# Results — Study 483 (Zero-Lag EMA)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **removing
the moving-average lag (Ehlers' de-lag) makes a timelier trend filter, so "long while price >
ZLEMA" beats a plain EMA of the same length** — encoded as a mechanical rule. The ZLEMA is
causal (``EMA_L(close + (close - close[lag]))``, ``lag = (L-1)//2``, ``L = 20``); the folklore
filter "long while price > ZLEMA" is sampled every 5 bars (non-overlap), entered at the **next
close** (one documented lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return on SPY/QQQ/IWM/
DIA/GLD. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce
every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **2,811** sampled `price > ZLEMA` in-state bars pooled across the 5 tapes (L = 20, step = 5) |
| Timing / costs | ZLEMA is causal; the long-state is read on the close, enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per trade |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — `price > ZLEMA` vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch ZLEMA-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ_rnd = ZLEMA − random; Δ_ema =
ZLEMA − plain-EMA (the head-to-head the thesis hinges on).

| horizon | n | ZLEMA | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ_rnd | plain-EMA | Δ_ema | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 2806 | +15.1 bps | 56% | +3.58 | +24.7 bps | **−9.6 bps** | +19.4 bps | −4.2 bps | +13.1 bps | −1.37 | 0.170 |
| 10-day | 2806 | +44.8 bps | 62% | +6.53 | +54.3 bps | **−9.5 bps** | +43.9 bps | +0.9 bps | +42.8 bps | −0.99 | 0.323 |
| 20-day | 2799 | +96.0 bps | 64% | +8.09 | +117.2 bps | **−21.2 bps** | +80.6 bps | +15.4 bps | +94.0 bps | −1.57 | 0.116 |
| 60-day | 2779 | +265.0 bps | 68% | +7.93 | +279.5 bps | **−14.6 bps** | +250.7 bps | +14.2 bps | +263.0 bps | −0.63 | 0.529 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks spectacular (**+8.09** at 20 days) —
but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index inherit the drift.
Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the `price > ZLEMA` filter is *worse* at every
horizon (Δ_rnd = −9.6 / −9.5 / −21.2 / −14.6 bps) and the difference **never clears the desk's
*t* ≥ 2 bar** — in fact the Welch *t* is **negative** at all four horizons. The trend filter
does not forecast: it merely re-collects a slice of the drift, less efficiently than a coin flip.

And the thesis: ZLEMA − plain-EMA (Δ_ema) is **−4.2 / +0.9 / +15.4 / +14.2 bps** — tiny, mixed
in sign, and never close to a meaningful margin. **Removing the lag buys essentially nothing.**

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — ZLEMA loses to random, and barely moves vs the plain EMA

| ticker | entries | ZLEMA | one-sample *t* | random | Δ_rnd | Δ_ema |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 566 | +88.0 bps | +3.82 | +115.6 bps | **−27.5 bps** | +7.3 bps |
| QQQ | 568 | +122.1 bps | +4.10 | +171.8 bps | **−49.7 bps** | +4.0 bps |
| IWM | 554 | +90.4 bps | +2.94 | +106.2 bps | **−15.8 bps** | +39.3 bps |
| DIA | 558 | +80.8 bps | +3.66 | +104.3 bps | **−23.6 bps** | +18.6 bps |
| GLD | 565 | +98.4 bps | +3.57 | +87.5 bps | **+11.0 bps** | +7.7 bps |

ZLEMA underperforms a dart-throwing entry in **4 of 5** names (only GLD edges +11 bps), and the
ZLEMA-minus-EMA delta is a small positive sliver everywhere (max +39 bps on IWM) — far too small
and far too noisy to call an edge of the de-lag. No coherent cross-sectional advantage: the
hallmark of relabelled drift, with the "zero-lag" twist adding nothing.

## The upcross foil — the bare ZLEMA cross whipsaws

The discrete *upcross* version of the rule (buy the bar price first crosses above the ZLEMA) is
even more clearly a beta capture, and the de-lag makes the cross jumpy:

| test | n | mean | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY ZLEMA upcross (H = 20) | 602 | +72.6 bps | 68% | +2.48 |

The high one-sample *t* (+2.48) is the index drift again; on a *planted* trend (synthetic
control below) the upcross banks **far less** than the steady `price > ZLEMA` filter, because
the extrapolated de-lag overshoots and the cross fires near tops. The de-lag does not buy a
timelier entry — it buys a noisier one.

## De-lag placebo — scramble the zero-lag correction, nothing changes

The decisive "is the de-lag doing anything?" test: keep the close, but **permute** the de-lag
offset ``close - close[lag]`` (same marginal, alignment destroyed) before re-running the same
EMA + filter. If ZLEMA's edge really came from the zero-lag correction, the scramble would
collapse the result.

| test | observed `price>ZLEMA` 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY de-lag scramble | +88.0 bps | **0.363** | 500 |

**36% of scrambled-de-lag forks match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.363). The specific
zero-lag correction carries no information — a random offset does about as well. "Removing the
lag adds edge" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real trend

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* persistent trend regime (knob `edge`), the same
`price > ZLEMA` filter behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine
"nothing there", not a dead detector. (And note the head-to-head: even where the trend is real,
the **plain EMA banks more** than the de-lagged ZLEMA.)

| planted edge | ZLEMA n | ZLEMA mean | win% | ZLEMA *t* | plain-EMA mean | plain-EMA *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.0** (no trend) | 403 | +0.3 bps | 47% | +0.01 | +18.3 bps | +0.55 |
| **2.0** (real planted trend) | 565 | +5,676.8 bps | 62% | **+4.94** | +9,589.1 bps | **+7.52** |

With no planted trend the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted trend
lights up at *t* = +4.94. The detector is live — and the plain EMA (*t* = +7.52) **beats** the
zero-lag version on the very effect ZLEMA was supposed to capture sooner.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The `price > ZLEMA` filter does **not** beat a drift-matched random
  baseline (ZLEMA − random = −9.6 / −9.5 / −21.2 / −14.6 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the Welch *t*
  is **negative** at every horizon, never near +2). The impressive one-sample *t*'s (20-day
  +8.09) are pure beta — the upward drift of long equity indices.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** No residual edge once the free drift is removed; costs only deepen
  the hole. You'd capture the same drift more cheaply and more fully by **holding the index**.
  Nothing to scale.
- **"Does removing MA lag buy anything?" — BUSTED.** ZLEMA minus the plain EMA it claims to
  improve on is **−4.2 / +0.9 / +15.4 / +14.2 bps** — tiny and mixed, never material; the de-lag
  placebo leaves the result intact (*p* = 0.363); and even on a *planted* trend the plain EMA
  banks more than the de-lagged line. The de-lag buys a noisier line, not a timelier edge.
